strengths: Provides a rigorous and clean formalization of recursive language models via a context-stack semantics (Definitions 1-4), distinguishing local vs. global space in a way that has clear practical implications (KV-cache offloading, active-context bound).

Establishes a coherent hierarchy of theoretical results: unbounded-depth recursion reaches TIME(2^O(S(n))) with O(S(n)) local space (Theorem 1), standard CoT is limited to roughly TIME(O(S(n))) (Theorem 2), and constant-depth recursion matches SPACE(S(n)), i.e., the power of optimal single-context/summarization strategies (Theorem 3). This cleanly separates recursion depth as the key resource governing expressivity.

Gives two independent proofs of the main theorem (direct recursive-function simulation of a TM, and an alternative via alternating Turing machines/Chandra-Kozen-Stockmeyer), together with an explicit sketch of Transformer realizability (constant-depth, O(log S(n))-precision), which grounds the abstract complexity results in concrete architectural feasibility.

Generalizes the minimal recursive model to a broad 'recursive agentic system' framework (oracle-Turing-machine scaffolds with least-fixpoint semantics) and proves an optimality result (Theorems 4-5): no more sophisticated multi-agent orchestration can exceed the power of the simple call/return mechanism under bounded active context. This is a nice unifying contribution connecting theory to real agentic system design (summarization, diffusion, prover/verifier examples all fit the framework).

The experimental result is striking: a fine-tuned 3B model substantially outperforms much larger frontier LLMs (GPT-4o, LLaMA3.3-70B, Qwen3-235B) on SAT solving, and shows favorable context-efficiency scaling (Figure 3), illustrating a genuine practical benefit of the proposed mechanism.

The paper is honest about limitations (error accumulation discussion in §6.3) and situates itself clearly relative to prior recursion-in-LM work, correctly identifying that shallow/constant-depth recursion approaches (concurrent works) are provably no more powerful than summarization.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation does not isolate the causal contribution of 'recursion' as claimed by the theory: there is no ablation comparing the recursive model to a standard CoT (depth-1) model fine-tuned on the same DPLL-derived reasoning traces/data, nor to a fine-tuned summarization-based baseline. Without this, the large accuracy gap over frontier LLMs could largely stem from high-quality supervised fine-tuning on task-specific search traces rather than the recursive context-management mechanism per se, undermining the central empirical claim that recursion is what enables the gains.

Experiments are limited to a single task (SAT), a single base model (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct), and no scaling study across recursion depth, model size, or SFT vs. RL training; evaluation sets are small (100 instances per difficulty) with no reported variance, limiting the strength/generality of the empirical conclusions.

The training data is generated by directly encoding a specific, hand-designed DPLL backtracking algorithm's trace as call/return sequences. This raises the concern that the model is essentially imitating a fixed algorithm rather than learning general-purpose recursive decomposition, which somewhat weakens the paper's broader claims about 'any computable problem is modularizable' being empirically validated.

Inference-efficiency and context-offloading claims (§6.1) are argued theoretically (FLOPs counting) but not measured empirically (e.g., real wall-clock latency/throughput with actual KV-cache offload/restore overhead), leaving the practical significance of the claimed GS/LS speedup unverified.

The optimality results for recursive agentic systems (Theorems 4-5) rely on specific assumptions (L-bounded execution, oracles computable within particular time/space bounds) that may not hold for many realistic multi-agent systems, so the practical scope of the 'optimality' claim is narrower than the framing in the main text suggests.

While the theoretical machinery is rigorous, it largely repurposes/extends well-established classical results (Savitch's recursive Turing machines, the Chandra-Kozen-Stockmeyer alternation theorem, prior FASP-to-Transformer compilation from Yang et al. 2025b) to the LLM/token-sequence setting; the conceptual novelty is primarily in the formalization and framing rather than fundamentally new complexity-theoretic insight, which is appropriately acknowledged but somewhat oversold in places (e.g., 'we identify recursion as a core principle... exclusive to modern agentic systems').

strengths: Provides a rigorous, general formalization of recursion in language models via a context-stack semantics (call/return), cleanly separating local vs. global space—a distinction with clear practical relevance (GPU memory vs. offloadable storage).

Strong theoretical results: two independent proofs (direct recursive-function simulation of TMs, and an alternative via alternating Turing machines/Chandra-Kozen-Stockmeyer) showing deep recursion achieves TIME(2^O(S(n))) with only O(S(n)) local space, an exponential separation from standard autoregressive models (Theorem 2) and from single-context/summarization approaches (Theorem 3).

The generalization to 'recursive agentic systems' via oracle Turing machines and least-fixpoint semantics is elegant, and the matching upper bounds (Theorems 4-5) showing the minimal call/return mechanism is already optimal among arbitrary recursive orchestrations is a nice, non-trivial complement to the lower-bound constructions.

Good connection to classical computation theory (Savitch's recursive TMs, nested stack automata) that contextualizes the novelty of applying recursion depth as an explicit resource for bounded-context Transformers.

Empirical results are compelling in magnitude: a fine-tuned 3B model substantially outperforms much larger frontier LLMs (GPT-4o, LLaMA3.3-70B, Qwen3-235B) on SAT across difficulty levels, and shows generalization to harder instances than trained on.
Reasonably detailed reproducibility material (appendix with data generation via DPLL, training hyperparameters, sample traces, and transformer construction sketches for the theoretical proofs).
weaknesses: The most important missing baseline is a same-size (3B) model fine-tuned on the same SAT data using standard (non-recursive) chain-of-thought traces. Without this, it's unclear how much of the reported gain over frontier LLMs is attributable to the recursive mechanism itself versus simply task-specific fine-tuning/domain adaptation.

Empirical validation is limited to a single synthetic task (SAT via DPLL-derived traces) with supervision that hands the model an explicit, hand-crafted recursive decomposition strategy; it does not demonstrate that models can learn or benefit from recursion on more open-ended/naturalistic long-horizon reasoning tasks where the decomposition is not given a priori.

No ablations isolating the contributions of the two practical variants used (prompt prefixing, question preservation) or of recursion depth/breadth on accuracy vs. context efficiency, despite these being discussed as theoretically consequential (e.g., depth-1 vs. constant-depth vs. unbounded).

No comparison against the other recursion/context-folding baselines discussed in Related Work (e.g., context-folding, RECAP, ADAPT) even though the theory explicitly predicts they should underperform deep recursion—an empirical test of this specific claim is absent.

The headline theoretical result (Theorem 1) requires recursion depth and total steps that are themselves exponential (or double-exponential without memoization) in S(n); while local space is small, practical latency/throughput implications of such deep call/return chains are only partially addressed (efficiency discussion in §6.1 assumes idealized KV-cache offloading with no recomputation cost).

No error bars, multiple seeds, or variance reporting for the SAT accuracy results, and evaluation set sizes (100 per difficulty) are modest, especially for measuring generalization to the 'hard' bucket.
